# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Reliable demand forecasting is foundational to the functioning of Family Planning Supply Chains (FPSC), directly shaping contraceptive availability, service delivery, and health outcomes [@hewage2025]. Even small improvements in availability can lead to measurable increases in uptake. For instance, having one additional method available can result in a 6.5% increase in contraceptive usage [@rosen2018modeling]. Yet, generating accurate forecasts in FPSC settings remains a persistent challenge due to volatile demand patterns, poor data quality, and operational disruptions such as frequent stockouts and service interruptions [@karimi2021; @devries2020]. In fact, fewer than half of health facilities in some settings maintain records in LMIS (Logistics Management Information System) that match their physical inventory counts [@karimi2021].

These structural and operational constraints frequently lead to censored demand data, periods where actual need is unobserved or underreported. In FPSC, two main forms of censorship arise (see @fig-ts_plot). First, **partial censorship** occurs during stockouts, where true demand exceeds available inventory and healthcare sites can only record sales up to the amount of stock on hand [@karimi2021]. Second, **full censorship** arises from service interruptions, including facility closures, under trained staff, or data collection failures, which prevent actual demand from being recorded at all [@hewage2025; @muyinda2015]. For example, a health facility might report zero demand because it was closed, even when products were available in the system and users needed them.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-ts_plot
#| out.width: "70%"
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Censorship scenarios in family planning supply chains."

synthetic_tsibble <- read_rds(here::here('data/tidy_data/synthetic_data.rds'))

# pick one series per

selected <- synthetic_tsibble |>
  filter(store == 'S51', product == 'P8')

# grab the full time‐slice for those series

plot_df <- synthetic_tsibble |>
  semi_join(selected, by = c("series_category","series_type","store","product")) |> 
  mutate(series_type     = str_to_sentence(series_type),
         series_category = str_to_sentence(series_category)) |> 
  group_by(series_category, series_type, store, product) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(period = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()


# build shading rectangles for each contiguous run of censorship

shade_df <- plot_df |>
  as_tibble() |> 
  arrange(series_category, series_type, store, product, period) |>
  group_by(series_category, series_type, store, product) |>
  mutate(
    run_id = cumsum(
      c(TRUE, censorship_type[-1] != censorship_type[-n()])  
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(series_category, series_type, store, product, run_id, censorship_type) |>
  summarize(start = min(period), end = max(period), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(censorship_type != "none")

# plot

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data = shade_df,
    aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = censorship_type), 
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.25) +
  
  geom_rect(data = shade_df |> 
              filter(start == end),
            aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, colour = censorship_type),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = NA,
            size = 0.5, alpha = 0.05, show.legend = FALSE) +
  
  geom_line(data = plot_df,
            aes(x = period, y = actual_demand, colour = "Actual", linetype = "Actual"),
            size = 0.7) +
  
  geom_line(data = plot_df,
            aes(x = period, y = observed_demand, colour = "Observed", linetype = "Observed"),
            size = 0.7) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Censorship type", values = c(censored = "#E69F00", disruption = "#0072B2"),
                    labels = c(censored   = "Stockout", disruption = "Interruption")) +
  
  scale_colour_manual(name = "Demand", 
                      values = c(Actual = "black", Observed = "red", censored = "#E69F00", disruption = "#0072B2"),
                      breaks = c("Actual", "Observed")) +
  
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Demand",values = c(Actual = "solid", Observed = "dashed")) +
  
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Demand") +
  theme_few(base_family = "Assistant", base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.border       = element_rect(colour = "lightgrey", fill = NA),
    panel.spacing      = unit(0.5, "lines")
  )



```

The failure to capture true demand results in systematically biased sales records and downward-biased forecasts [@wecker1978; @trapero2024]. This situation is referred to as a **lost sales context** in inventory management [@heese2010], where the true extent of unmet demand remains unknown. Ignoring censorship leads to under-ordering, increased risk of stockouts, and a **spiral-down effect**, where misinformed replenishment decisions lead to further unmet need and lost sales over time [@cooper2006].

While the lost sales framework is widely used in inventory theory to distinguish between systems with and without backordering, it rarely considers how those losses arise from structural data issues. In FPSC, lost sales refer to unmet consumption or distribution opportunities, demand that goes unrecorded due to stockouts or service interruptions, rather than commercial transactions. In such systems, demand cannot be backordered; if a user visits during a stockout, that opportunity is permanently lost. For example, methods like emergency contraceptives are time-sensitive, and their need does not carry over. Here, censorship becomes the mechanism through which demand is lost. Ignoring this distinction risks underestimating both need and service risk in replenishment models.

The consequences of stockouts and service interruptions in FPSC are far-reaching. When contraceptives are unavailable, users may be turned away or forced to forgo their preferred method [@sedgh2016]. Even when alternatives exist, users may be reluctant to switch due to concerns about side effects, reduced effectiveness, lack of awareness, or partner opposition [@karimi2021]. Moreover, users in developing countries, particularly rural areas, may travel substantial distances (30 minutes to a full day) and incur significant travel costs (25%-250% of daily living expenses) in search of health commodities. High search costs mean users often return home empty-handed if the product is out of stock [@RHSC2016; @TakeStock2017]. This leads to rising unmet demand and an increase in unintended and closely spaced pregnancies, which are estimated at 111 million annually in developing countries [@sully2020]. Over 60% of these unintended pregnancies end in abortion, with nearly half of them being unsafe, contributing to \rev{hospitalization and maternal mortality} [@bearak2020].

Despite the recognised importance of maintaining adequate contraceptive stocks, our discussions with supply chain planners in the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) highlighted that stockouts remain a pressing challenge within the FPSC, including in countries such as Côte d’Ivoire and Ethiopia. To gain a deeper understanding, we conducted a field visit to Ethiopia in February 2025, where we held discussions with supply chain planners and program managers from the Ethiopian Pharmaceutical Supply Service (EPSS) and the Ministry of Health. 

During our field visit, we conducted interviews and observational visits at multiple levels of the EPSS, from healthcare facilities and regional hubs to the national warehouse. Practitioners consistently emphasised that stockouts remain common, not just due to funding or shipment delays, but because demand remains poorly captured. In many cases, facilities fail to report on time, forcing regional planners to extrapolate needs or allocate stock based on outdated consumption records. These workarounds often result in mismatches, where sites either receive insufficient quantities or are supplied with products they do not urgently need. At the national level, planners from EPSS highlighted that these reporting gaps make it difficult to generate accurate aggregate demand for procurement planning. As a result, procurement orders are often misaligned with actual needs, compounding the stockout problem at scale. This underscores the importance of addressing demand censorship not just as a data issue, but as a structural barrier to supply chain reliability.

The existing solutions to tackle the lost sales context remain ad hoc, depending on available information and specific demand assumptions (see @tbl-literature) [@trapero2024]. A core challenge is the unobserved nature of lost sales, causing biases in data and complicating forecasting and inventory optimisation [@beutel2012; @pedregal]. Many methods assume constant censoring levels or overlook operational realities such as reporting delays and service interruptions. Simple time series models struggle with missing data and with capturing complex temporal patterns like trends, seasonality, or external shocks [@hewage2025].

In practice, demand planners often intervene, adjusting system-generated forecasts or revising order quantities to account for local realities not captured in the data [@siemsen2025; @hewage2025]. These adjustments may reflect anticipated deliveries, outreach campaigns, or known reporting gaps, and are often made to prevent stockouts. However, such interventions are informal, vary across sites, and are rarely supported by formal tools. However, prior studies show that under lost sales, such adjustments often anchor on available data and under-correct for unobserved need [@feiler2013; @tong2018]. While behavioural tools have been proposed to mitigate this bias, their use in operational settings remains limited [@syntetos2016]. This highlights the need for forecasting approaches that are structurally aligned with how demand is recorded and censored in FPSC, reducing reliance on manual workarounds.

At the same time, optimal inventory policies under lost sales are computationally intensive due to the curse of dimensionality, where decisions depend on the full inventory pipeline [@bijvank2011]. Traditional models often assume that excess demand is backordered, an assumption that does not hold in FPSC, where demand is typically lost if unfulfilled [@karimi2021; @hewage2025]. Moreover, the historical separation of forecasting and inventory research limits understanding of how demand estimation translates into actual service levels [@goltsos2022].

To address these limitations, we propose the Truncated Conformal Kalman Filter (TCKF), a probabilistic forecasting framework specifically designed to model censored demand and support inventory decision-making in FPSC. The method integrates a Tobit Kalman Filter with a conformal prediction layer. The Kalman filter component allows for time series modelling in the presence of partial and full censorship, while accounting for trends, shocks, and missing observations. The conformal layer provides calibrated, distribution-free prediction intervals, enabling more robust, uncertainty-aware inventory planning. While individual studies have addressed aspects of forecasting, inventory, or service access, no prior work in FPSC has offered an integrated approach that links demand estimation with inventory implications and downstream public health impact. To our knowledge, this is the first such framework applied to FPSC. The key contributions of our study are:

-   We introduce TCKF, a probabilistic forecasting method that combines Tobit Kalman filtering with conformal prediction to estimate censored demand under stockouts and service interruptions, and we evaluate its performance against established benchmarks.

-   We evaluate the proposed method on both synthetic and empirical data from Côte d’Ivoire, comparing performance not only in terms of forecast accuracy, but also in downstream inventory reliability and public health outcomes, a contribution that connects forecasting to inventory management and ultimately to public health impacts.

-   \rev{We introduce the Unified Relative Score (URS) to evaluate the downstream operational utility of forecasts. By employing an asymmetric, quadratic penalty structure, the URS explicitly captures the critical trade-off between severe service failures and disproportionate inventory accumulation, providing a highly decision-relevant measure of performance in resource-constrained settings.}

All code and datasets are publicly available to support reproducibility and to enable adaptation and generalisation, both across FPSC in diverse developing-country contexts and in other supply chains that contend with censored demand. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related literature and positions our work. Section 3 outlines the proposed model. Section 4 describes the experiment setup. Sections 5 and 6 present the numerical and empirical results, respectively. Section 7 concludes with key insights, limitations, and directions for future research.
